claims.text: An MLIP can be trained on a limited set of ab initio data representing both solid and liquid phases.
Explicit corrections can make an MLIP retain anharmonic vibrational contributions.
Explicit corrections can make an MLIP retain electron–vibration coupling contributions.
The proposed surrogate can accurately compute high-temperature fusion free energies.
The proposed surrogate can accurately compute entropy contributions associated with fusion.
The method will reduce cost by at least an order of magnitude relative to both explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD.
Elemental and simple binary metals near melting exhibit significant anharmonic lattice vibrations in the solid phase.
Both solid and fluid phases of the target systems exhibit significant electron–vibration coupling near melting.
A limited number of high-temperature ab initio MD runs can train a potential that supports cheaper long-timescale simulations.
An ab initio-parameterized MLIP can capture atomic interactions in an alloy.
The MLIP can capture anharmonic and electron–vibration energetic contributions in both target phases.
Learning the relevant free-energy contributions permits rapid sampling of configuration space.
The resulting sampling has accuracy comparable to explicit ab initio MD.
The MLIP route eliminates the need for full-scale ab initio MD and expensive TOR-TILD evaluations.
The method retains the free energies and vibrational entropy of both solid and liquid phases.
MLIP free energies will be within approximately 10% of explicit ab initio MD results.
MLIP-derived melting temperatures and latent heats will be within approximately 10% of explicit ab initio MD results.
The MLIP workflow will be approximately 10 times less costly than TOR-TILD.
Explicit ab initio MD free-energy evaluations and TOR-TILD are highly accurate but computationally very costly.
The approximately 10% error and 10-fold speed estimates are based on preliminary studies.

contradictions.description: The central prediction requires roughly a 10-fold or greater cost reduction, but the falsification rule rejects the method only when the reduction is below 2-fold. A result such as a 3- to 5-fold speedup would fail the stated prediction while still passing the stated falsification rule.
